---
title: Configuration
---

This document describes the configuration settings as an interface for
both the Python classes as well as the file that contains the settings.
For the Python classes, this document includes the signature,
docstrings, and some pseudocode as a potential implementation. It
primarily serves as a reference for us to develop from and track what
has been finished and what remains to be done.

{{< include /docs/includes/_design-status.qmd >}}

## Overview

Given that a Data Package can either be very simple with only a few data
resources or complex with many resources and detailed schemas with
hundreds of resource fields, Flower needs to be configurable to
accommodate different use cases for displaying the wide range of
metadata. Displaying all the metadata in a single file may be sufficient
for a simple Data Package, but is impractical for more complex ones.
That's where the configuration comes in to be able to customise the
generated documentation output.

Flower's configurations are meant to be used to control what type of
files are output for the human-readable documentation of the
`datapackage.json` metadata, how those the contents of those files are
structured (determined by the templates), what contents are included in
those files, and where those files are output.

The configuration is split into two main parts:

-   The top-level configuration that is represented by the `Config`
    class, the settings under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table in
    `pyproject.toml`, or the settings at the top level of the
    `_flower.toml` file. These settings dictate whether to use a
    built-in style or a custom style, along with the location of the
    template files for any custom style.
-   The lower-level configuration that is represented by one or more
    `Section` classes, the `[[tool.seedcase-flower.section]]` tables in
    `pyproject.toml`, or the `[[section]]` tables in `_flower.toml`.
    These settings dictate what contents of the `datapackage.json`
    (**not individual properties**) are included in each section of the
    documentation and where those sections are output.

The configuration files are read in and directly mapped to the Python
classes. So, we'll describe most of the design details in the Python
classes below.

As already mentioned in the [CLI design document](cli.qmd), one design
choice we're making is that configuration can only happen either
directly in the Python classes or in the configuration files, but not on
the CLI. This keeps the CLI simpler, especially considering that some
configuration options can be complex (e.g. multiple sections with
different content types). This would make the CLI complex, more
difficult to implement and parse, and less reproducible for those
wanting to re-build the documentation later (or if a collaborator wants
to re-build it). That way, as long as the configuration file is included
in the project, the same documentation can be built consistently when
using `seedcase-flower build`.

## Python classes

### {{< var planned >}} `Config`

This class contains all the configuration settings for styling the
documentation. It represents a one-to-one mapping to the settings
provided in the `_flower.toml` or `pyproject.toml` file.

It contains settings for whether to use a built-in style or to use a
custom one with custom Jinja2 templates, along with the list of sections
to create for the output. A description of each attribute is listed
below in the docstring of the pseudocode.

Flower will use [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/)
to generate the human-readable documentation from the `datapackage.json`
metadata. The advantage of using Jinja2 is that you can create any type
of file output because it first gets rendered by Jinja2. For example,
you can create `.qmd` files if the Jinja2 template ends in `.qmd.jinja`.
This gives a lot of flexibility in the types of outputs a user can
create. They aren't limited to a specific markup language or file
format. It also makes it easier for us to develop Flower and to add new
built-in styles, as we don't need to do any checks on the type of output
file itself or the content, as we let Jinja2 handle that.

The contents of the the `template_dir` path must contain one Jinja2
template file for each `Section.contents` type used in the `sections`
attribute. For example, if a `Section` has
`contents=["package", "resources"]` and
`template_dir=Path("templates/)`, then there must be two files:
`templates/package.md.jinja` and `templates/resources.md.jinja` (if
outputting to `.md` files) Flower won't check if you've included
template files with different names than what is allowed by
`Section.contents`, but will restrict the types of names you can use in
the `Section.contents` attribute.

Theoretically, a user could create a custom style that lists all the
metadata found in the `datapackage.json` file in a single Jinja template
file, as long as it was called `package.md.jinja` (or whichever output
format they wanted).

When making a Jinja2 template file, we designed Flower to pass the full
`datapackage.json` file into the template file to keep it easier for us
to implement and easier to create templates as we can make use of [JSON
path syntax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSONPath). But that also
means that each property must be listed in full following the JSON path
syntax. For example, if we wanted to list all the contributors first
name in the `contributors.md.jinja` template, we would use Jinja2 loops
on all contributors with `.contributors[ID].given_name` (where `ID` is
the number for the item in the contributors list).

As will be described later, we intentionally restrict the types of names
you can use in the `Section.contents` attribute to ensure that there is
a clear mapping between what is available in the `datapackage.json` file
and what can be output in the documentation.

### Pseudocode: `Config` class

```` python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal, Optional

# TODO: Might have to use pydantic instead to run basic checks when creating the class...?
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    """Configuration settings for styling the metadata.

    TODO: Include link when implemented

    See the [design](LINK) for an explanation on the decisions for how Config is
    designed. See the [guide](LINK) on how to set up custom styles and sections.
    See `Section` for more details on how to set up sections.

    Attributes:
        style (Literal["quarto-book", "custom"]): Whether to use a built-in
            style or to use a custom one.  Default is the "quarto-book" style. If
            you want to use a custom style, set this to "custom" and provide the
            path to the templates in `template_dir`.
        template_dir (Optional[Path]): If `style` is "custom", this should be
            the directory path to the [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/)
            template files. The directory **must** contain one template file for each
            `Section.contents` type used in the `sections` attribute.
        sections (Optional[list[Section]]): List of `Section` classes that dictate one or
            more sections to create for the output, including output path and content types.

    Examples:
        ``` python
        # A config using the built-in `quarto-book` style
        config = Config(
            style="quarto-book"
        )

        # A custom config with only `package` contents in one section
        config = Config(
            style="custom",
            template_dir=Path("templates"),
            sections=[
                Section(
                    output_path=Path("docs/"),
                    contents=["package"]
                )
            ]
        )

        # A custom config with multiple sections and content types
        config = Config(
            style="custom",
            template_dir=Path("templates"),
            sections=[
                Section(
                    output_path=Path("docs/package.qmd"),
                    contents=["package", "license", "contributors"]
                ),
                # Section that outputs each resource as a file in the `resources/` folder
                Section(
                    output_path=Path("docs/resources/"),
                    contents=["resources"]
                )
            ]
        ```
    """
    style: Literal["quarto-book", "custom"] = "quarto-book"
    template_dir: Optional[Path] = None
    sections: Optional[list[Section]] = None
````
:::

### {{< var planned >}} `Section`

The main purpose of `Section` is to allow creating separate "sections"
of the documentation, in this case, separate files to display different
parts of the `datapackage.json` metadata. There are two attributes:
`output_path` and `contents`. Each has some specific decision patterns
to them that increase their complexity but also allow for some powerful
flexibility.

For the `output_path`, this dictates what the name of the file or output
folder should be. But it isn't as simple as "this outputs content to
this given file". That's because specific properties of the
`datapackage.json` file are arrays (or Python lists). For instance, you
can have more than one data resource, which itself has many properties
that also could have many of them such as having many fields in its
schema. So we need some way to output a list of data resources to a
corresponding list of output files. That's where some complexity comes
in.

When a property that we want to display is a list, like resources, we
can set an output path as a folder with the special `{}` whisker
brackets in place of where the file name should be to allow creating
multiple files for each resource. Since we need some way to replace the
`{}` with the actual name of the property to display, we can only allow
this behaviour when the given property has a `name` sub-property. The
reason we decided to use the `name` property is because it has
requirements in the Data Package specification that make it ideal for
using as a file name, specifically that it can't have spaces and must be
all lowercase.

To show how this might look, imagine we wanted to create individual
files for each resource in the `docs/resources/` folder. We would set
`output_path="docs/resources/{resource-name}.qmd"`. Why `resource-name`
and not `name`? Because if we wanted to create individual files for each
field in the schema of each resource, we would need some way to
differentiate between the two `name` properties. So we could use
`docs/resources/{resource-name}/fields/{resource-schema-field-name}.qmd`
in this case.

<!-- TODO: Not sure how this might be implemented in the Jinja templates. -->

When setting a multi-file output, the properties used within the Jinja2
template must use `{content-id}` format. For example, if we wanted to
output one file for each resource with an `output_path` like
`resources/{resource-name}.qmd`, then the corresponding
`template/resource.qmd.jinja` file must use Jinja2 variables that
reference a resource's properties with the JSON path syntax of
`.resources[{resource-id}].title` (for the `title` property of each
resource). Then Flower will loop through each resource property and
insert the number for that item in the resource. In this case, if there
were two resources, Flower would resolve it to `.resources[0].title` in
one output template file and `.resources[1].title` in another output
template file.

For the `contents` attribute, we decided on using a specific set based
on whether a property in the `datapackage.json` is a list or whether it
represents a distinct "entity" that might be worthy of having a
dedicated page of documentation. Based on that, the properties as JSON
paths are `.contributors`, `.licenses`, `.sources`, `.resources`,
`.resources[*].schema`, `.resources[*].sources`,
`.resources[*].licenses`, and `.resources[*].schema.fields`. But there's
also the top level `.` (all the Data Package properties). So simplifying
those, the `contents` we allow are `package` (for the `.` top-level),
`contributors`, `licenses`, `sources`, `resources`, and for individual
resource properties `resource-schema`, `resource-licenses`,
`resource-sources`, and `resource-schema-fields`. So semantically, the
`package` content and it's corresponding, e.g., `package.md.jinja`
template file could contain all properties listed in its template file,
but `licenses` would only contain the properties found under
`.licenses`. However, Flower won't parse and check if other properties
are used outside of their semantic place, for example if the `.title`
top-level property was used in the `licenses` content template file.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
### Pseudocode: `Section` class

```` python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pathlib import Path

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Section:
    """A section of the documentation with specific `datapackage.json` properties.

    TODO: add link below.

    See the [design](LINK) for an explanation on the decisions for the design of
    `Section`. See the [guide](LINK) on how to set up custom styles and sections.
    See `Config` for more details on the top-level settings.

    Attributes:
        output_path (Optional[Path]): The output path for this section. Can be `None`
            when a style outputs to the terminal such as when using `view()`.
            If a directory is provided, files will be created for each content type that has
            a `name` property (e.g. `resources` or `resource-schema-fields`) For example,
            if `output_path` is `Path("docs/")` and `contents` is `["resources"]`,
            then each resource will be output to `docs/{resource_name}.md` (or whichever output
            format is used in the Jinja2 template files). If a file path is provided, all contents
            within the `Section` will be output to that single file.
        contents (list[Literal[...]]): List of content to include in this
            section. Must be the name of one or more of the content listed. Each of these must
            have a corresponding Jinja2 template file in the `template_dir` of the same name (e.g.
            `package.md.jinja` or `resources.rst.jinja`).

    Examples:
        ``` python
        # A section that contains only the package and contributors content types,
        # saved to the `docs/package.qmd` file.
        Section(
            output_path=Path("docs/package.qmd"),
            contents=["package", "contributors"]
       )
       ```
    """
    output_path: Optional[Path] = None
    # Needs to be one or more of the following strings.
    # TODO: Not sure if this is the best/correct way to ensure option is only one of these.
    contents: list[Literal[
        "package", "contributors", "licenses", "sources", "resources", "resource-schema",
        "resource-licenses", "resource-sources", "resource-schema-fields"
    ]]
````

## Configuration file

<!-- TODO: Replace link with our own decision "why TOML" post -->

We use a configuration file to ensure that how the documentation is
built is explicitly defined and reproducible whenever someone simply
uses the `seedcase-flower build` command. This way, anyone who has
access to the Data Package and the configuration file can re-build the
documentation in the same way. We use TOML for the file format since
there are [more advantages to it for storing configuration
settings](https://www.anbowell.com/blog/an-in-depth-comparison-of-json-yaml-and-toml/).
The two biggest advantages to TOML for us are that you can use comments
(with `#`) and the content is treated purely as data (e.g. YAML can
contain content that can be parsed as code and executed).

The configuration file contains a one-to-one mapping with the `Config`
and `Section` classes described above. The configuration file can either
be named `_flower.toml` or be included in the `pyproject.toml` file
under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table. The ordering of which
configurations are used is as follows:

1.  If an argument is given to `style` in the `build()` CLI function,
    use that.
2.  If not, search for a `_flower.toml` file in the working directory
    and read the configurations if it exists.
3.  If `_flower.toml` does not exist, search for a `pyproject.toml` file
    in the working directory and read the configurations under the
    `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table if it exists.
4.  If neither file exists, use the default configurations as defined in
    the `Config` class, which represents the default built-in style.

We chose to override the configurations if given from the CLI to prevent
potential configuration conflicts between settings in the configuration
file and settings given on the CLI. This way, it is clear which ordering
the settings are applied.

### {{< var planned >}} `_flower.toml`

The `_flower.toml` file contains the configuration settings for Flower.
For a simple configuration using the built-in style, the file can be as
simple as:

``` {.toml filename="_flower.toml"}
style = "quarto-book"
```

For such a simple configuration, it would be easier to give the CLI
`--style` option the `quarto-book` argument instead. But using the
configuration file makes it clear which style was used, for
reproducibility and transparency purposes.

More complex customisations are where a configuration file becomes
necessary. For example, if you want to set custom settings using your
own Jinja2 templates along with the custom sections where the content is
output, the `_flower.toml` file could look like:

``` toml
# This is optional if `template-dir` is given.
style = "custom"
# This would have at least the files:
# -   package.qmd.jinja
# -   contributors.qmd.jinja
# -   resources.qmd.jinja
# -   resource-schema-fields.yml.jinja
templates-dir = "path/to/templates/"

# The `index.qmd` would contain the combined `package` and `contributors` contents
# from the Jinja2 templates.
[[section]]
output-path = "docs/index.qmd"
contents = [
    "package",
    "contributors"
]

# This would create one file per resource in the `docs/resources/` folder.
# E.g. `docs/resources/demographics.qmd`, `docs/resources/blood.qmd`, etc.
[[section]]
output-path = "docs/resources/"
contents = ["resources"]

# This would create a YAML file for each resource with its schema fields.
# The `{resource-name}` variable would be replaced with the name of each resource.
# In this example, this would allow you to use a Quarto listing for the fields:
# https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html#yaml-listing-content
[[section]]
output-path = "docs/resources/{resource-name}/schema-fields.yml"
contents = ["resource-schema-fields"]
```

### {{< var planned >}} `pyproject.toml`

We allow the configuration settings to be set in the `pyproject.toml`
file under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table for convenience,
particularly if the Data Package is also a Python project that needs to
use `pyproject.toml`. This way, they don't need to create an additional
configuration file just for Flower.

The same configuration settings can also be provided in the
`pyproject.toml` file under the `[tool.seedcase-flower]` table. Taking
the complex example from the `_flower.toml` above, the `pyproject.toml`
version would look like:

``` toml
[tool.seedcase-flower]
style = "custom"
template_dir = "templates/"

[[tool.seedcase-flower.section]]
output_path = "docs/package.qmd"
contents = [
    "package",
    ...
]

[[tool.seedcase-flower.section]]
output_path = "docs/resources/"
contents = ["resources"]

[[tool.seedcase-flower.section]]
output-path = "docs/resources/{resource-name}/schema-fields.yml"
contents = ["resource-schema-fields"]
```
:::
